# **II. Project Introduction** {#ii.-project-introduction}

## **1\. Overview** {#1.-overview}

**CareBridge – A Maternal and Early Childhood Healthcare Platform** is developed to support wome

n's healthcare throughout three major stages: **preconception, pregnancy, and postpartum with early childcare**.

The platform enables users to access verified medical information, receive guidance from verified healthcare professionals, follow personalized care plans, and monitor maternal and infant health indicators. CareBridge also supports family connectivity, allowing family members to monitor the mother's health status and provide timely support whenever needed.

Through features such as **verified health information moderation, expert consultation, health indicator monitoring, and personalized care planning**, CareBridge helps users better prepare for every stage of the maternal journey, reduce missed essential care activities, and promote a safer and healthier pregnancy and early motherhood experience.

### **1.1 Project Information** {#1.1-project-information}

* Project name: **CareBridge \- A Maternal and Early Childhood Healthcare Platform**  
* Project code: MECHP  
* Group name: SEP490\_G79  
* Software type: Web Application, Mobile Application

## **2\. Product Background** {#2.-product-background}

### **2.1 Global Overview** {#2.1-global-overview}

Maternal and early childhood healthcare has become one of the highest global public health priorities. The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) emphasize that maternal and child healthcare should be managed as a **continuum of care**, beginning before conception and continuing throughout pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum recovery, and early childhood. Despite significant progress in reducing maternal and child mortality, millions of women and children continue to experience preventable health complications each year. These challenges highlight the need for continuous health monitoring, reliable medical information, timely intervention, and coordinated healthcare throughout the maternal journey. 

#### ***2.1.1 Preconception Care*** {#2.1.1-preconception-care}

##### **2.1.1.1 Why Is Preconception Care Important?** {#2.1.1.1-why-is-preconception-care-important?}

Preconception care is the process of improving the health of women and men before pregnancy to increase the chance of a healthy pregnancy and reduce the risk of complications for both the mother and the baby. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), preconception care is a package of interventions that aims to identify and address health conditions, behavioral factors, and social risks before pregnancy. These interventions can improve the health of women and men, pregnancy outcomes, and child health. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), the goal of preconception care is to reduce risks to the mother, fetus, and newborn by optimizing health, managing modifiable risk factors, and providing education about a healthy pregnancy.

[https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2019/01/prepregnancy-counseling](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2019/01/prepregnancy-counseling)

Preconception care can help identify or reduce many important risks, including:

* Neural tube defects caused by folic acid deficiency.  
* Complications related to diabetes, hypertension, thyroid disease, and obesity.  
* Exposure to alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs, and medications that may harm the fetus.  
* Rubella, hepatitis B, HIV, and sexually transmitted infections.  
* Genetic diseases in the family.  
* Modifiable causes of preterm birth, low birth weight, and pregnancy complications.

[https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2019/01/prepregnancy-counseling](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2019/01/prepregnancy-counseling)

##### **2.1.1.2 Access to Preconception Care Worldwide** {#2.1.1.2-access-to-preconception-care-worldwide}

Although the benefits of preconception care are well established, the use of these services remains low in many countries. A 2025 systematic review including 6,808 women from 14 studies in Ethiopia reported a pooled preconception care utilization rate of 26%. This means that about three out of four women in the included studies did not use preconception care services. This finding represents data from Ethiopia and should not be interpreted as a global estimate.

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40057689/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40057689/)

In the United States, a study of women enrolled in Medicaid found that only 23.6%–28.1% received or reported receiving at least one preconception care service during the year before pregnancy.

[PubMed – Preconception care utilization among women with Medicaid (2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38032882/)

Studies have also identified several common barriers to preconception care, including:

Limited knowledge about preconception care.

Not visiting healthcare facilities before pregnancy.

Insufficient training of healthcare professionals.

*  Unclear responsibility for providing preconception care services.  
*  Limited time, tools, clinical guidelines, resources, and financial support.

[PubMed – Barriers and facilitators to preconception care](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30096578)

In addition, a 2025 meta-analysis found that education level, access to healthcare services, and previous counseling were strongly associated with knowledge and practice of preconception care. Women who had received preconception counseling were significantly more likely to adopt recommended preconception care practices.

[PubMed – Knowledge, attitudes and practices toward preconception care](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41127552/)

##### **2.1.1.3 Consequences of Poorly Controlled Medical Conditions Before Pregnancy** {#2.1.1.3-consequences-of-poorly-controlled-medical-conditions-before-pregnancy}

Many chronic diseases and infectious diseases can increase the risk of serious complications if they are not identified and managed before pregnancy.

**Diabetes**

Poorly controlled diabetes increases the risk of preeclampsia, stillbirth, fetal overgrowth, birth injury, and neonatal hypoglycemia. According to WHO, diabetes affects approximately one in six pregnancies worldwide, which is equivalent to more than 21 million women every year.

Sources:

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240117044](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240117044)

[https://www.who.int/news/item/14-11-2025-who-launches-global-guidelines-on-diabetes-during-pregnancy-on-world-diabetes-day](https://www.who.int/news/item/14-11-2025-who-launches-global-guidelines-on-diabetes-during-pregnancy-on-world-diabetes-day)

**Hypertension**

Hypertensive disorders during pregnancy can lead to preeclampsia, eclampsia, stroke, kidney failure, placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and stillbirth. WHO estimates that preeclampsia affects approximately 3–8% of women giving birth worldwide. Hypertensive disorders caused about 16% of all maternal deaths in 2023, equal to approximately 42,000 deaths.

Sources:

[https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/pre-eclampsia](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/pre-eclampsia)

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008793](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008793)

**Anaemia**

Anaemia during pregnancy increases the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, reduced iron stores in newborns, and poor tolerance to blood loss during childbirth.

According to WHO, in 2023:

* 30.7% of women aged 15–49 years had anaemia.  
* 35.5% of pregnant women had anaemia.  
* 30.5% of non-pregnant women had anaemia.

Sources:

[https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/anaemia](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/anaemia)

[https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/anaemia\_in\_women\_and\_children](https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/anaemia_in_women_and_children)

**Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)**

Untreated sexually transmitted infections can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, and mother-to-child transmission.

According to WHO:

* More than 1 million curable STIs occur every day.  
* There were approximately 374 million new infections in 2020\.  
* In 2022, about 1.1 million pregnant women had syphilis, resulting in more than 390,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Sources:

[https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/sexually-transmitted-infections-%28stis%29](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/sexually-transmitted-infections-%28stis%29)

[https://www.who.int/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/stis/prevention/mother-to-child-transmission-of-syphilis/](https://www.who.int/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/stis/prevention/mother-to-child-transmission-of-syphilis/)

##### **2.1.1.4 Recommendations from WHO and Other Health Organizations** {#2.1.1.4-recommendations-from-who-and-other-health-organizations}

WHO, ACOG, and CDC recognize preconception care as an important preventive approach that should begin before pregnancy.

**Health examination and risk assessment.** Individuals planning a pregnancy should be assessed for chronic diseases, reproductive and family history, current medications, vaccination status, infectious diseases, and genetic risks. Early assessment allows healthcare professionals to control existing medical conditions, adjust potentially harmful medications, and identify factors that may affect the health of the mother or fetus.

[Source: ACOG – Prepregnancy Counseling](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2019/01/prepregnancy-counseling)

**Lifestyle modification.** CDC recommends taking 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, avoiding alcohol, tobacco, and illicit drugs, reducing exposure to harmful substances, and maintaining a healthy body weight. WHO also identifies nutrition, tobacco use, mental health, infectious diseases, and environmental risks as important areas for intervention before conception.

Sources:

[CDC – Planning for Pregnancy](https://www.cdc.gov/pregnancy/about/index.html)

[WHO – Preconception Care to Reduce Maternal and Childhood Mortality and Morbidity](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241505000)

**Preconception counselling and health education.** ACOG and CDC recommend integrating preconception counselling into routine preventive healthcare. Counselling should address reproductive planning, healthy behaviours, safe medication use, birth spacing, vaccination, and the appropriate use of professional healthcare services. This process helps individuals and couples understand their health risks, make informed decisions, and prepare physically and psychologically for a healthy pregnancy.

[Source: CDC – Recommendations to Improve Preconception Health and Health Care](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5506a1.htm)

#### ***2.1.2 Antenatal Care (ANC)*** {#2.1.2-antenatal-care-(anc)}

##### **2.1.2.1 Importance of Antenatal Care** {#2.1.2.1-importance-of-antenatal-care}

Antenatal care is the process of monitoring, screening, prevention, counselling, and support throughout pregnancy. According to WHO, ANC helps identify conditions and complications such as hypertension, pre-eclampsia, anaemia, gestational diabetes, infections, and abnormalities in fetal development at an early stage. Appropriate and timely interventions contribute to protecting maternal and fetal health and improving the pregnancy experience.

[WHO – Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience, 2016, with selected recommendations updated through 2022:](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/)

However, pregnancy is not managed only during clinical visits. Between contacts with healthcare professionals, pregnant women may need to monitor their weight, blood pressure, symptoms, fetal movements, nutrition, and medication use. They must also decide whether a change is a normal physiological feature of pregnancy or a sign that requires professional care. Therefore, the periods between visits may create gaps in access to information, health monitoring, and risk recognition.

ACOG – Tailored Prenatal Care Delivery for Pregnant Individuals, 2025:

[https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals)

##### **2.1.2.2 Global Access to Antenatal Care** {#2.1.2.2-global-access-to-antenatal-care}

UNICEF data updated in 2024 indicate that approximately 87% of pregnant women worldwide received at least one ANC visit with a skilled health professional, while only about 70% received at least four visits. Coverage of four or more visits was approximately 57% in West and Central Africa and 58% in South Asia. These figures demonstrate that considerable regional disparities in continuity of antenatal care remain.

UNICEF Data – Antenatal Care, updated in 2024:

[https://data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/antenatal-care/](https://data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/antenatal-care/)

These figures are still based on the earlier minimum standard of four visits, whereas WHO now recommends at least eight ANC contacts. Moreover, the number of visits alone does not fully reflect service quality or whether a pregnant woman actually receives the necessary examinations, counselling, and interventions.

WHO – Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience, 2016:

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/)

Common barriers to ANC include cost, distance to healthcare facilities, limited transportation, inadequate insurance coverage, lack of information, family-care responsibilities, and shortages of healthcare workers. A 2025 systematic review also identified long waiting times, language barriers, stigma, mental health difficulties, violence, and disrespectful experiences in healthcare settings. These factors can lead women to initiate ANC late, miss appointments, or discontinue care.

Barriers to Timely and Adequate Antenatal Care: A Systematic Review, 2025:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41454267/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41454267/)

WHO – Maternal Mortality, updated in 2025:

[https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/maternal-mortality](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/maternal-mortality)

##### **2.1.2.3 Need for Accurate Health Information and Risks of Unverified Information** {#2.1.2.3-need-for-accurate-health-information-and-risks-of-unverified-information}

Pregnant women have substantial information needs concerning screening tests, medications, nutrition, childbirth, newborn care, and the management of unusual symptoms.

A 2020 systematic review of 79 studies found that more than 90% of pregnant women in the reviewed studies used the Internet, primarily to obtain health information, learn about pregnancy and childbirth, and seek social support. The findings illustrate the strong demand for pregnancy-related information that is convenient and accessible.

PubMed – Internet Use by Pregnant Women Seeking Pregnancy-Related Information: A Systematic Review, 2020:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32989946/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32989946/)

A 2022 systematic review similarly found that the Internet was the most frequently reported information source in 15 of the 24 included studies. However, the authors identified a gap between the information pregnant women needed and the information they could actually find or understand. Access therefore depends not only on the amount of available content but also on its clarity, relevance, and reliability.

Lu et al. – Understanding Information Needs and Barriers to Accessing Health Information Across All Stages of Pregnancy, 2022:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35188477/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35188477/)

The widespread availability of information does not guarantee its accuracy. A 2023 scoping review of pregnancy applications identified safety concerns relating to the evidence base, transparency, reliability, privacy, and the ability to provide content appropriate to individual users.

Carrandi et al. – Safety Considerations for Assessing the Quality of Apps Used During Pregnancy, 2023:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37675058/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37675058/)

A 2024 systematic review also identified misinformation on social media regarding COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy, particularly claims about fertility, vaccine safety, and fetal effects. Unverified information can increase anxiety, distort risk perception, and influence healthcare decisions.

Malik et al. – Social Media Misinformation about Pregnancy and COVID-19 Vaccines, 2024:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38484723/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38484723/)

Online information for pregnant women should therefore be moderated, transparently sourced, and based on scientific evidence. It should complement consultation with qualified healthcare professionals rather than replace clinical examination, diagnosis, or professional guidance.

##### **2.1.2.4 Consequences of Inadequate Care and Monitoring** {#2.1.2.4-consequences-of-inadequate-care-and-monitoring}

When ANC is initiated late or is not maintained adequately, opportunities to detect and manage risks early may be reduced. Pregnant women may miss blood pressure measurement and proteinuria testing for pre-eclampsia; gestational diabetes testing; screening for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B; anaemia detection; ultrasound for pregnancy dating; or monitoring of fetal growth. This can delay intervention when maternal or fetal conditions become serious.

WHO – Recommendations on Interventions Along the Life Course: Maternal:

[https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal](https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal)

A 2023 systematic review in sub-Saharan Africa identified attendance at only zero to four ANC visits and poor-quality ANC as modifiable risk factors associated with stillbirth. The findings indicate that access must be accompanied by adequate service quality, completion of essential tests, and timely intervention when risks are identified.

Aminu et al. – Determinants of Stillbirths in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review, 2023:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37272228/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37272228/)

Misinformation can also affect decisions concerning medication, vaccination, nutrition, and the timing of seeking care. However, pregnancy complications should not be attributed directly to Internet information in every case. The more defensible concern is that misinformation may delay care-seeking, increase anxiety, or encourage inappropriate health decisions.

Malik et al. – Social Media Misinformation about Pregnancy and COVID-19 Vaccines, 2024:

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38484723/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38484723/)

##### **2.1.2.5 Recommendations from WHO and Other Health Organizations** {#2.1.2.5-recommendations-from-who-and-other-health-organizations}

WHO recommends a minimum of eight ANC contacts, with the first contact taking place during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. More frequent contacts create additional opportunities for health professionals to assess maternal and fetal health, identify risks, and provide stage-appropriate guidance.

WHO – Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience, 2016:

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/)

ANC should include assessment of medical history and risk factors; monitoring of blood pressure, weight, and fetal growth; screening for anaemia, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, pre-eclampsia, and gestational diabetes; and tests appropriate to each stage of pregnancy.

WHO – Recommendations on Interventions Along the Life Course: Maternal:

[https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal](https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal)

WHO recommends at least one ultrasound examination before 24 weeks of gestation to estimate gestational age, support the detection of multiple pregnancy or certain fetal abnormalities, and improve pregnancy management.

WHO – Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience, 2016:

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/)

Other key measures include nutritional counselling, iron and folic acid supplementation, tetanus vaccination according to previous immunization status, birth preparedness, and education about danger signs that require timely medical attention.

WHO – Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience, 2016:

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241549912/)

In 2025, ACOG recommended a comprehensive assessment of medical and social needs before 10 weeks of gestation or as soon as a pregnant individual enters care. The ANC plan should be personalised according to health status, pregnancy risk, access to services, and individual needs.

ACOG – Tailored Prenatal Care Delivery for Pregnant Individuals, 2025:

[https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals)

ACOG also stated that home monitoring and telehealth may be used as part of ANC when users receive appropriate instruction, use reliable devices, understand abnormal thresholds, and have a clear method of contacting healthcare professionals. These approaches are supplementary and do not fully replace in-person visits.

ACOG – Tailored Prenatal Care Delivery for Pregnant Individuals, 2025:

[https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals)

WHO released the Digital Adaptation Kit for Antenatal Care in 2021, describing care workflows, core health data, follow-up schedules, decision-support logic, and functional requirements for digital systems. The document demonstrates that technology can support implementation of ANC recommendations, but digital systems must be grounded in clinical guidance and must not replace examination, diagnosis, or treatment by healthcare professionals.

WHO – Digital Adaptation Kit for Antenatal Care, 2021:

[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020306](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020306)

#### ***2.1.3 Postnatal Care (PNC)*** {#2.1.3-postnatal-care-(pnc)}

##### **2.1.3.1 Why Is Postnatal Care Important?** {#2.1.3.1-why-is-postnatal-care-important?}

WHO defines the postnatal period as the first six weeks after childbirth. This period begins immediately after the baby is born. It is an important time for the mother to recover, for the newborn to adapt to life outside the womb, and for health problems to be identified early. Mothers and families need clear information, counselling, and continuous support from qualified healthcare professionals.

[WHO – Recommendations on Maternal and Newborn Care for a Positive Postnatal Experience, 2022](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240045989)

During this period, the mother should be monitored for bleeding, infection, blood pressure problems, mental health conditions, and breastfeeding difficulties. The newborn should be assessed for breathing, body temperature, feeding ability, jaundice, infection, and other danger signs. Timely care supports early detection of complications and helps families provide safe care for the newborn.

Sources: WHO – Postnatal Care Interventions for Mothers and Newborns

[https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal](https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal)

WHO and UNICEF recommend starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. They also recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and continued breastfeeding until two years of age or longer, together with suitable complementary foods.

Source: WHO – Breastfeeding

[https://www.who.int/health-topics/breastfeeding](https://www.who.int/health-topics/breastfeeding)

##### **2.1.3.2 Current Status of Postnatal Care Worldwide** {#2.1.3.2-current-status-of-postnatal-care-worldwide}

Although postnatal care is essential, many mothers and newborns do not receive timely health checks. According to UNICEF, in 2023, approximately 69% of mothers and 68% of newborns received a postnatal health check within the recommended period. This means that about 31% of mothers and 32% of newborns did not receive timely postnatal care. WHO also reports that more than three in ten women and newborns do not receive care during the first days after childbirth.

Source: UNICEF Data – Newborn Care, updated in 2024

[https://data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/newborn-care](https://data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/newborn-care)

Source: WHO – Quality Care in the First Weeks after Childbirth, 2022

[https://www.who.int/news/item/30-03-2022-who-urges-quality-care-for-women-and-newborns-in-critical-first-weeks-after-childbirth](https://www.who.int/news/item/30-03-2022-who-urges-quality-care-for-women-and-newborns-in-critical-first-weeks-after-childbirth)

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of low- and middle-income countries reported that the pooled use of postnatal care services in the included studies was approximately 55.4%. Major barriers included economic conditions, education level, place of residence, distance to healthcare facilities, knowledge of postnatal care, and family support. This result should not be interpreted as a global rate.

Source: Midwifery – Multifactorial Determinants of Postpartum Care Uptake in Low- and Middle-Income Countries, 2025

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40701041/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40701041/)

When professional support is limited, many mothers search for information on the Internet and social media. A survey of 349 women in Belgium found that 90.5% used the Internet to find information about themselves or their babies after childbirth. Although 82.7% considered the information useful, the average quality rating was only 5.3 out of 10\. About 80% reported that online information influenced their decisions. These findings do not represent the global population, but they show a strong need for reliable postnatal information.

Source: Midwifery, 2017

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28324809/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28324809/)

The quality of online content is also inconsistent. A 2025 study evaluated 80 popular Instagram posts about breastfeeding. Only 38.8% were completely accurate, while 36.3% were mostly or completely inaccurate. Content created by healthcare professionals had significantly higher quality.

Source: Journal of Human Lactation, 2025

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41017325](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41017325)

##### **2.1.3.3 Consequences of Inadequate Postnatal Care or Unverified Information** {#2.1.3.3-consequences-of-inadequate-postnatal-care-or-unverified-information}

For the Mother

Inadequate postnatal care reduces the opportunity to detect postpartum haemorrhage, infection, hypertension, and mental health conditions at an early stage. Postpartum haemorrhage can progress quickly and become life-threatening without timely diagnosis and treatment. WHO reports that postpartum haemorrhage causes nearly 45,000 deaths worldwide each year.

Source: WHO, FIGO and ICM – Global Recommendations on Postpartum Haemorrhage, 2025

[https://www.who.int/news/item/05-10-2025-global-health-agencies-issue-new-recommendations-to-help-end-deaths-from-postpartum-haemorrhage](https://www.who.int/news/item/05-10-2025-global-health-agencies-issue-new-recommendations-to-help-end-deaths-from-postpartum-haemorrhage)

Postnatal infection can develop into sepsis, which may cause organ failure, death, or long-term health effects. The WHO Global Maternal Sepsis Study found that infection contributed to death or a near-death condition in approximately 11 women per 1,000 live births during hospitalization.

Source: WHO – Maternal Infections in Health Facilities, 2020

[https://www.who.int/news/item/27-04-2020-maternal-infections-in-health-facilities](https://www.who.int/news/item/27-04-2020-maternal-infections-in-health-facilities)

Mental health should also be monitored after childbirth. WHO estimates that approximately 13% of women who have recently given birth experience a mental health disorder, mainly depression. This proportion may reach 19.8% in developing countries. Without identification and support, these conditions may affect self-care, newborn care, and the relationship between the mother and baby.

Source: WHO – Perinatal Mental Health

[https://www.who.int/teams/mental-health-and-substance-use/promotion-prevention/perinatal-mental-health](https://www.who.int/teams/mental-health-and-substance-use/promotion-prevention/perinatal-mental-health)

For the Newborn

WHO reports that 2.3 million newborns died during the first 28 days of life in 2022\. This was equal to approximately 6,500 deaths each day and represented 47% of all deaths among children under five. The main causes included complications of premature birth, complications during childbirth, infections, and congenital conditions.

Source: WHO – Newborn Mortality, 2024

[https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/newborn-mortality](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/newborn-mortality)

Without postnatal examinations, danger signs such as poor feeding, rapid breathing, fever, low body temperature, reduced responsiveness, or jaundice may be missed. Parents may also receive insufficient guidance about breastfeeding, umbilical cord care, keeping the baby warm, and vaccination schedules. UNICEF considers health checks during the first two days after birth an important opportunity to identify risks and teach families how to care for the newborn.

Source: UNICEF Data – Newborn Care

[https://data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/newborn-care/](https://data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/newborn-care/)

WHO and UNICEF report that approximately 48% of infants under six months were exclusively breastfed in 2024\. The organizations estimate that improving breastfeeding rates could save more than 820,000 children each year. Therefore, inaccurate information or insufficient professional breastfeeding support may affect infant nutrition and care decisions.

Source: WHO and UNICEF – Equal Access to Breastfeeding Support, 2024

[https://www.who.int/news/item/31-07-2024-on-world-breastfeeding-week--unicef-and-who-call-for-equal-access-to-breastfeeding-support](https://www.who.int/news/item/31-07-2024-on-world-breastfeeding-week--unicef-and-who-call-for-equal-access-to-breastfeeding-support)

There is currently no global estimate of the number of postnatal complications or deaths directly caused by online misinformation. Therefore, unverified information should be considered a factor that may influence care behaviour, delay help-seeking, or lead to unsuitable decisions, rather than a direct cause of every complication.

### **2.2 Viet Nam Background** {#2.2-viet-nam-background}

Viet Nam has made considerable progress in maternal and child healthcare, as reflected in relatively high rates of antenatal care attendance, facility-based delivery, and postnatal care. However, differences in economic conditions, place of residence, ethnicity, health literacy, and access to technology continue to affect the quality and continuity of care. In addition, many families still experience difficulties in accessing reliable health information, managing health data, and coordinating care from the preconception period through early childhood.

Source: WHO – Viet Nam Country Health Data

[https://data.who.int/countries/70](https://data.who.int/countries/704)4

Source: UNFPA Viet Nam – Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights

[https://vietnam.unfpa.org/en/topics/sexual-reproductive-health-and-right](https://vietnam.unfpa.org/en/topics/sexual-reproductive-health-and-rights)s

#### ***2.2.1 Reproductive, Maternal, and Early Childhood Health in Viet Nam*** {#2.2.1-reproductive,-maternal,-and-early-childhood-health-in-viet-nam}

The Viet Nam Sustainable Development Goal Indicators on Children and Women Survey 2020–2021 found that 97% of women received antenatal care at least once from skilled health personnel, while 88.2% completed at least four visits. Approximately 96.3% of women delivered in a healthcare facility, and 96.1% of live births were attended by skilled health personnel. In addition, 88.1% of mothers and 88.5% of newborns received a health check within two days after childbirth.

Source: General Statistics Office of Viet Nam and UNICEF – Viet Nam SDGCW Survey 2020–2021

[https://www.unicef.org/vietnam/reports/viet-nam-sdg-indicators-children-and-women-survey-2020-202](https://www.unicef.org/vietnam/reports/viet-nam-sdg-indicators-children-and-women-survey-2020-2021)1

Although national coverage is high, substantial disparities remain between population groups. Only 10.6% of Mong women completed at least four antenatal visits, compared with 95.2% of Kinh and Hoa women. The proportion of Mong women delivering in a healthcare facility was only approximately 37%, while only 29.1% received a postnatal health check. These findings indicate that maternal healthcare services are not accessed equally in mountainous, remote, and ethnic-minority communities.

Source: General Statistics Office of Viet Nam, UNICEF, and UNFPA – Findings on Antenatal and Postnatal Care

[https://vietnam.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/info1\_anc\_eng\_6\_pages\_0.pd](https://vietnam.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/info1_anc_eng_6_pages_0.pdf)f

Health concerns continue after childbirth. In 2022, WHO estimated that the neonatal mortality rate in Viet Nam was 10.47 deaths per 1,000 live births and that the under-five mortality rate was 20.43 deaths per 1,000 live births. The Ministry of Health also reported that 18.2% of children under five experienced stunting in 2023, with higher rates recorded in the Northern Midlands and Mountainous region and the Central Highlands.

Source: WHO – Viet Nam Country Health Data

[https://data.who.int/countries/70](https://data.who.int/countries/704)4

Micronutrient deficiencies also remain an important concern. The 2019–2020 National Nutrition Survey found that 63.5% of pregnant women had zinc deficiency. The median urinary iodine concentration among pregnant women was also below the level recommended by WHO. These findings indicate that women need access to reliable guidance on nutrition and appropriate micronutrient supplementation.

Source: Ministry of Health – Results of the 2019–2020 National Nutrition Survey

[https://moh.gov.vn/en/tin-noi-bat/-/asset\_publisher/3Yst7YhbkA5j/content/bo-y-te-cong-bo-ket-qua-tong-ieu-tra-dinh-duong-nam-2019-202](https://moh.gov.vn/en/tin-noi-bat/-/asset_publisher/3Yst7YhbkA5j/content/bo-y-te-cong-bo-ket-qua-tong-ieu-tra-dinh-duong-nam-2019-2020)0

#### ***2.2.2 Gaps in Maternal and Early Childhood Healthcare*** {#2.2.2-gaps-in-maternal-and-early-childhood-healthcare}

Nationally representative data on the use of preconception care services in Viet Nam remain limited. However, a study involving 100 women planning a pregnancy and 200 pregnant women found that 62% had limited health literacy, while only 5% had adequate health literacy. Although 94% believed that prenatal supplements were beneficial, 64% were not convinced that these products were safe. Because the study was conducted online, its findings are not representative of all women in Viet Nam. Nevertheless, they indicate knowledge gaps before and during pregnancy.

Source: Le et al. – Awareness of Nutrition and Supplements Among Pregnant and Preconception Women: A Real-World Study in Vietnam, 2023

PubMed: [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37908636](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37908636/)/

Postnatal mental health also requires greater attention. A review of 18 studies conducted in Viet Nam reported postpartum depression rates ranging from 8.2% to 48.1%. This wide range resulted from differences in study locations, assessment periods, participant characteristics, and screening instruments. Therefore, it should not be interpreted as a single national prevalence rate. However, the findings demonstrate a genuine need for postnatal mental-health screening and psychological support.

Source: Nguyen et al. – The Rate and Risk Factors of Postpartum Depression in Vietnam From 2010 to 2020: A Literature Review, 2021

PubMed: [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34777111](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34777111/)/

DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2021.731306

Childhood immunisation has improved considerably, but some children still do not complete the recommended vaccination schedule. WHO and UNICEF estimated that approximately 40,000 children did not receive the third dose of the diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccine in 2024, while approximately 27,000 children did not receive the first measles vaccine dose. These figures demonstrate the continuing need to strengthen appointment reminders, follow-up, and communication with families.

Source: WHO and UNICEF – Progress in Childhood Immunisation in Viet Nam, 2025

[https://www.who.int/vietnam/news/detail/16-07-2025-viet-nam-achieves-remarkable-progress-childhood-immunization--who-and-unicef-repor](https://www.who.int/vietnam/news/detail/16-07-2025-viet-nam-achieves-remarkable-progress-childhood-immunization--who-and-unicef-report)t

Reliable national data are currently unavailable regarding the proportion of women who miss healthcare appointments, forget medical tests, lose health records, or experience insufficient coordination among family members. Therefore, these issues should be treated as gaps requiring further investigation rather than being presented as established national statistics for Viet Nam.

#### ***2.2.3 Access to Health Information and Misinformation*** {#2.2.3-access-to-health-information-and-misinformation}

Internet access is relatively widespread among women of reproductive age. The Viet Nam SDGCW Survey 2020–2021 found that 81.3% of women aged 15–49 had used the Internet during the three months preceding the survey, while 79.7% used it at least once per week. However, Internet use was higher in urban areas and considerably lower in rural areas, the Central Highlands, and the Northern Midlands and Mountainous region.

Source: General Statistics Office of Viet Nam and UNICEF – Mass Media, Communications, and Internet Report

[https://www.unicef.org/vietnam/media/8696/file/Mass%20media%20%26%20ICT.pd](https://www.unicef.org/vietnam/media/8696/file/Mass%20media%20%26%20ICT.pdf)f

The ability to use the Internet does not necessarily mean that users can accurately understand and evaluate health information. A study in Viet Nam found that many users continued to have limited health literacy despite regularly searching for information online. Educational level, place of residence, and the frequency of online health-information seeking were associated with users’ ability to understand and apply health-related content.

Source: Tran et al. – Health and eHealth Literacy in Vietnam: Evidence from a National Survey, 2026

PubMed: [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41830724](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41830724/)/

DOI: 10.1016/j.pec.2026.109583

In a study involving women planning a pregnancy and pregnant women, 77% of Vietnamese participants considered healthcare professionals to be a reliable source of information. However, they also obtained information from relatives and friends at a rate of 47%, websites at 36%, and online forums at 34%. This pattern indicates that professional information exists alongside informal online content.

Source: Real-World Insights on Nutritional Awareness and Behaviors Among Preconception and Pregnant Women in Three Asia-Pacific Countries, 2024

[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11135049](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11135049/)/

There is currently limited research in Viet Nam directly measuring the amount of misinformation concerning pregnancy, the postnatal period, and childcare on Facebook, TikTok, or YouTube. However, UNICEF has reported that rumours and vaccine misinformation may affect parental confidence and vaccination decisions. Therefore, misinformation should be regarded as a factor that may influence healthcare behaviour, but it should not be presented as the direct cause of every adverse health outcome.

Source: UNICEF Viet Nam – Immunisation and Vaccine Misinformation

[https://www.unicef.org/vietnam/immunizatio](https://www.unicef.org/vietnam/immunization)n

#### ***2.2.4. Legal Framework and Basis for Application Development*** {#2.2.4.-legal-framework-and-basis-for-application-development}

**Legal Framework**

– Professional Practice License Requirements

Health consultations provided through CareBridge must be conducted by healthcare professionals holding valid practice licenses. The application must verify their professional qualifications and licenses before allowing them to provide consultations to users.

Source: Law on Medical Examination and Treatment No. 15/2023/QH15, Article 2, Clauses 4–5, PDF page 2, content lines 1–7.

[https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2023/02/15luat.signed.pdf](https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2023/02/15luat.signed.pdf)

– Users’ Rights Regarding Personal Data Processing

CareBridge users must be clearly informed about the purposes for which their personal data is collected and processed. Users have the right to consent to, refuse, or withdraw their consent to the processing of their personal data.

Source: Law on Personal Data Protection No. 91/2025/QH15, Article 4, Clause 1, Points a–d, PDF page 3, content lines 1–13.

[https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2025/7/91qh.signed.pdf](https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2025/7/91qh.signed.pdf)

– Storage of Evidence of User Consent

CareBridge must retain evidence of user consent, including the identity of the consenting user, the time of consent, and the approved content. The application must not preselect consent options or present information in a manner that may mislead users.

[Decree No. 356/2025/NĐ-CP, Article 6, Clauses 1–3, PDF pages 5–6. Methods of providing consent through an application are specified on page 5, content lines 18–27, while requirements for storing evidence of consent are specified on page 6, content lines 3–11.](https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2026/01/356-nd.signed.pdf)

Basis for Application Development

– Guidelines of the Vietnamese Ministry of Health

This document provides the basis for developing preconception care content, including risk assessment, BMI, nutrition, folic acid supplementation, vaccination, health examinations, and pregnancy planning.

[Decision No. 1139/QĐ-BYT – Guidelines on Reproductive Healthcare, section on preconception care.](https://vnpa.moh.gov.vn/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/QD-1139-Tai-lieu-huong-dan-cham-soc-SKSS.pdf)

– WHO Antenatal Care Guidelines

This document provides the basis for developing the antenatal care schedule, health-monitoring activities for each stage of pregnancy, and appointment reminder functions. WHO recommends an antenatal care model involving a minimum of eight contacts.

 [WHO Recommendations on Antenatal Care for a Positive Pregnancy Experience, PDF page 1, lines 17–33 and 40–50.](https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/reproductive-health/maternal-health/anc.pdf?sfvrsn=5e2c740e_2)

– WHO Maternal Health Interventions

This source provides the basis for identifying health information and indicators that should be monitored during pregnancy, including blood pressure, weight, BMI, nutrition, iron and folic acid supplementation, medical tests, vaccination, and warning signs.

[WHO – Recommendations on Interventions Along the Maternal Life Course, Maternal Health Interventions section.](https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/handbooks/programme-manager-s-handbook-mncah/recommendations-on-interventions-along-life-course/maternal)

– Reference Information from Tu Du Hospital

The Tu Du Hospital resource provides the basis for developing consultation content related to BMI, body weight, and important health considerations before and during pregnancy.

Source: Tu Du Hospital – Health consultation information related to BMI and pregnancy.

[https://www.tudu.com.vn/en/article41000/article41405/article20254/](https://www.tudu.com.vn/en/article41000/article41405/article20254/)

#### ***2.2.5. Market Demand & User Pain Points*** {#2.2.5.-market-demand-&-user-pain-points}

##### **2.2.3.1. Context and Overview** {#2.2.3.1.-context-and-overview}

Available literature, product analysis, and preliminary project observations indicate practical gaps in maternal and early childhood care in Viet Nam. Although mothers and babies receive medical checks during clinic or hospital visits, most daily care activities take place at home. In this environment, families must remember instructions, monitor health changes, manage medical records, and make everyday parenting decisions with very limited professional support.

Currently, important care-related information is heavily fragmented across paper documents, smartphone photo galleries, personal notes, chat applications, and informal advice from relatives. When parents have urgent questions about symptoms, infant care, breastfeeding, vaccination, nutrition, or postpartum recovery, they rely heavily on public social media groups. While these open communities offer emotional comfort, they also expose families to dangerous unverified advice, unsafe home-care recommendations, hidden advertising, and confusing personal opinions.

The absence of a trusted digital health community creates major problems. Users frequently forget clinic appointments or vaccination milestones, lose important medical documents, miss early warning signs, and struggle to separate personal anecdotes from professional medical facts. Furthermore, families find it difficult to coordinate daily caregiving tasks smoothly among mothers, spouses, grandparents, and other caregivers.

![][image2]

##### **2.2.3.2. User Pain Points** {#2.2.3.2.-user-pain-points}

a) Pre-pregnancy Women 

* **Lack of preconception medical knowledge:** Difficulty accessing structured, certified guidelines on necessary genetic screenings, lifestyle adjustments, and vital nutrient intake prior to conception.  
* **Inconsistent scheduling and cycle tracking:** High risk of forgetting essential vaccination timelines, preconception clinical checkups, or accurately tracking menstrual cycles for ovulation window optimization.  
* **Fragmented medical histories:** General screening records, gynecological lab results, and personal health data are stored across loose papers, making long-term baseline health evaluation difficult.  
* **Unscientific lifestyle and wellness planning:** Struggles with designing a balanced nutrition and adequate rest routine targeted specifically for boosting fertility and maternal readiness.  
* **Delayed direct doctor accessibility:** Inability to quickly reach out to certified specialists for minor pre-pregnancy symptoms, queries, or medical guidance.  
* **Absence of a trusted support community:** Lack of a secure, moderated peer network to share experiences, anxieties, and authentic advice regarding the preparation journey.

b) Pregnant Women 

* **Complexity in tracking pregnancy milestones:** Difficulties in keeping up with different medical examination checklists and dynamic testing requirements assigned to specific gestational weeks.  
* **Non-centralized maternity profiles:** Ultrasound images, blood work reports, and genetic test outcomes are scattered, creating risk of information loss and lack of interoperability.  
* **Inability to track health metrics chronologically:** Hard to systematically analyze long-term patterns in weight gain, blood pressure, or blood sugar levels over the months.  
* **Delayed recognition of danger signs:** Lack of automated guidance to identify critical home-care red flags \- such as preeclampsia indicators or abnormal fetal kicks \- leading to delayed emergency responses.  
* **Lack of instantaneous clinical support:** Absence of a rapid virtual consulting channel with attending doctors when sudden, alarming physiological changes occur at home.  
* **Unoptimized nutritional management:** Struggles to adapt daily dietary intake to match specific gestational demands, often leading to gestational diabetes or nutritional deficiencies.  
* **Anxiety over labor preparation:** High stress and confusion regarding what medical documents, newborn essentials, and physical supplies to prepare for delivery day.

c) Postpartum Mothers 

* **Deficit in postpartum recovery and infant care knowledge:** Overwhelmed by unverified, conflicting advice on postpartum wound healing, lactation techniques, and safe newborn soothing methods.  
* **Missed immunization and infant wellness tracks:** High risk of missing the baby’s continuous vaccination timelines and pediatric growth monitoring milestones amidst a chaotic routine.  
* **Mental health risks and severe burnout:** Susceptibility to postpartum depression, intense emotional anxiety, and psychological imbalance due to sleep deprivation and poor time management.  
* **Unstructured infant routine tracking:** Difficulties in accurately logging and monitoring the baby’s daily sleep windows, feeding volumes, and diaper change frequencies.  
* **Siloed mother-and-baby health data:** Medical records for both the recovering mother and the newborn are stored independently and disjointedly across separate physical folders.  
* **Financial tracking inefficiencies:** Challenges in monitoring and budgeting accumulating household expenses for diapers, formulas, medical checkups, and infant care utilities.

d) Spouses and Family Members 

* **Information black holes regarding schedules:** Total lack of direct, real-time access to the mother’s clinical appointment timelines, prenatal tests, or baby immunization calendars.  
* **Inability to gauge maternal emotional stress:** Disconnect from the mother's daily mental health state and psychological anxiety levels, hindering timely emotional support.  
* **Absence of immediate anomaly alerts:** No automated mechanism to receive urgent notifications when the mother or infant experiences dangerous physiological fluctuations at home.  
* **Lack of actionable caregiving knowledge:** Insufficient training and authenticated medical insights on how to properly care for a pregnant spouse or a fragile newborn.  
* **De-centralized medical history overview:** Family members cannot quickly retrieve or review past medical records of the mother and child during home emergencies.  
* **Inaccurate financial forecasting:** Difficulties in tracking, organizing, and predicting the collective costs of pregnancy management, child rearing, and healthcare services.

### **2.3. Conclusion – Why CareBridge is needed** {#2.3.-conclusion-–-why-carebridge-is-needed}

The analysis presented in Sections **2.1** and **2.2** shows that maternal and early childhood healthcare extends far beyond hospital visits. Throughout the journey from preconception to pregnancy, postpartum recovery, and early childhood, women, families, and caregivers require continuous support to manage their health effectively.

Three fundamental needs emerge from the current challenges. First, users need access to **accurate and trustworthy medical information** to make informed decisions and reduce the risk of misinformation. Second, they need **timely support from verified healthcare professionals** to obtain reliable guidance when health concerns arise. Third, they need **a structured and personalized care journey** that helps them manage health records, monitor health indicators, receive reminders, and complete important healthcare activities at the right time.

Although healthcare organizations and government regulations provide important clinical guidelines and legal frameworks, these needs are not fully addressed in everyday practice. Health information remains fragmented, home-based monitoring is limited, and many families still face difficulties accessing reliable healthcare resources and coordinating their care.

To address these gaps, **CareBridge** is designed as an integrated maternal and early childhood healthcare platform. It centralizes maternal and child health records, provides verified medical information, connects users with licensed healthcare professionals, supports personalized care journeys, delivers timely reminders, and enables continuous monitoring of maternal and child health indicators.

Rather than replacing healthcare providers, CareBridge complements existing healthcare services by improving continuity of care, strengthening communication between families and healthcare professionals, and helping users better manage every stage of the maternal and early childhood healthcare journey. Through these capabilities, CareBridge contributes to a safer, more connected, and more proactive approach to maternal and child healthcare.

## **3\. Existing Systems** {#3.-existing-systems}

### **3.1 “Trợ lý mẹ bầu. Theo dõi thai kỳ” (Pregnancy and Due Date Tracker) App** {#3.1-“trợ-lý-mẹ-bầu.-theo-dõi-thai-kỳ”-(pregnancy-and-due-date-tracker)-app}

![][image3]

**Description:**

Pregnancy (by Wachanga) is a comprehensive pregnancy tracking and mobile journal application designed to support expectant mothers throughout their 40-week gestation period. The system operates as a personal digital assistant, providing daily and weekly medical-based insights, tracking fetal development benchmarks, and offering interactive tools to monitor the mother's physical changes and labor readiness. It functions primarily as a standalone B2C mobile application for parents, utilizing local and cloud storage to build a personalized pregnancy diary.

**Link:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.wachanga.pregnancy](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.wachanga.pregnancy)

**Main features:**

* **Weekly & Daily Pregnancy Information:** Delivers curated medical articles, tips, and fetal development updates customized to the exact gestational age.  
* **Fetal Development Visualizer:** Displays illustrative images and sizing charts (comparing the fetus to familiar fruits/objects) to visualize growth.  
* **Weight & Health Tracker:** Monitors the mother's weight gain and body mass index (BMI) fluctuations against standard pregnancy charts.  
* **Kick Counter (Fetal Movement):** An interactive digital clicker to record, log, and analyze the frequency and patterns of baby kicks.  
* **Contraction Timer:** A precise stopwatch tool to measure the duration and frequency of labor contractions, helping mothers determine when to head to the hospital.  
* **Infant/Baby Shopping Checklist:** Pre-configured and customizable to-do lists to help parents prepare necessary newborn gear and hospital bags.  
* **Digital Journal & Diary:** Allows mothers to log daily moods, physical symptoms, blood pressure readings, and personal photos/notes.

**Pros:**

* Scientific and highly structured content, providing clear guidance on what to expect during each specific week of pregnancy.  
* The UI is clean, intuitive, and highly accessible for pregnant women, minimizing complexity during data entry.  
* The built-in contraction timer and kick counter eliminate the need for manual pen-and-paper tracking or installing separate single-utility apps.  
* Visual size comparisons (fruit models) create an engaging, emotionally positive user experience for expectant parents.  
* Lightweight and stable baseline performance on most standard Android and iOS devices.

**Cons:**

* Rigid "Happy Path" design: The system lacks an adaptive or sensitive mechanism to handle negative pregnancy outcomes (e.g., miscarriage or stillbirth). If a tragic event occurs, the app continues to push generic promotional notifications and growth milestone celebrations, which can trigger severe emotional distress.  
* Siloed user data (Lack of multi-user sync): In the standard tier, data is locked to a single device/account, making it difficult for husbands or family members to seamlessly co-track or view real-time logs without sharing credentials.  
* Intrusive monetization: Based on real-world user reviews on the Google Play Store, the free version contains frequent, disruptive video advertisements and heavily locks essential tracking tools behind a restrictive paywall.  
* Disconnected from healthcare ecosystems: The app operates in complete isolation from medical facilities. Health logs, symptoms, and weight data cannot be synced via API to private clinic dashboards, forcing users to manually transcribe data or read it out loud to their doctors during physical checkups.  
* Generic nutritional and lifestyle guidance: Articles and meal suggestions follow a standardized global/Western blueprint, which is often not localized or budget-friendly for users in specific regional markets like Vietnam.

### **3.2  Pregnancy+ | Tracker App** {#3.2-pregnancy+-|-tracker-app}

![][image4]

**Description:**

Pregnancy+ is a premium B2C mobile application and medical journal engine designed to track human gestation from blastocyst to full-term birth. Serving a global user base, the system’s primary architectural differentiator is its interactive, high-fidelity 3D fetal development models that support multi-ethnic visualization, zooming, and rotation. The application operates as a standalone cloud-connected system that can be personalized, allowing the primary user to share access logs and data streams with grandparents or other designated family members.

**Link:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.hp.pregnancy.lite](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.hp.pregnancy.lite)

**Main features:**

* **Interactive 3D Fetal Models:** Highly detailed, rotatable, and zoomable 3D renders representing embryonic and fetal growth week-by-week, including guided walkthroughs and tap-to-move animations.  
* **Multi-Category Baby Size Guide:** Visualizes estimated fetal volume and length by mapping metrics to dynamic asset groups (Fruits, Animals, and Sweets/Sweets).  
* **Multi-User Sync & Share:** Personalization system allowing external invitations for family members to view synchronized pregnancy progression updates.  
* **Clinical Information Pipeline:** In-house daily articles, medical blogs, and deep-dive health advice authored by licensed midwives, lactation consultants, and obstetricians.  
* **Biometric Data Logs & Utilities:** Core tracking utilities including a Due Date Calculator, Kick Counter, Pregnancy Weight Log (graphing BMI curves), and a Contraction Timer.  
* **Organizational Planner:** Module incorporating a Digital Birth Plan exporter, Hospital Bag checklist (categorized for Mother, Support Person, and Baby), Appointment Calendar, and a Newborn Shopping List.  
* **My Bump Diary:** A media storage module for uploading and organizing sequential gestational photos into a digital pregnancy timeline.

**Pros:**

* Industry-leading visual engagement through highly sophisticated and realistic 3D renderings that significantly enhance emotional attachment.  
* Multi-ethnic customizer for 3D assets allows users to adapt the visual model to match their specific demographic profile.  
* Credible, expert-vetted knowledge base reduces the spread of misinformation commonly found on open internet forums.  
* Seamless multi-user sharing architecture allows fathers and extended family members to participate in the tracking cycle without duplicate account setups.  
* Clean entry UI and high system stability with over 80 million downloads globally.

**Cons:**

* **Forced layout manipulation & UX Friction:** Based on real-world user reviews, the UI frequently shuffles free utilities (like weight loggers) to randomized positions on the home screen to intentionally drive user visibility toward premium paywalled modules.  
* **High-barrier Paywall:** Essential long-term tracking capabilities, historical data exports, and extensive educational modules (such as the 3D Documentary walkthroughs) are locked behind an expensive subscription wall or require viewing excessive video ads.  
* **Zero Healthcare/EHR Integration:** The app remains completely isolated from hospital or laboratory Enterprise Systems. All diagnostic data (such as actual 2D/4D ultrasound measurements or lab results) must be manually transcribed by the user, leading to data fragmentation between the app and actual medical records.  
* **Privacy & Aggressive Data Harvesting:** According to App Store data disclosures, the platform collects and links highly sensitive user profiles, usage metrics, and coarse location data to the user's identity for third-party advertising and targeted product profiling.  
* **Glitchy Community Features:** Discussion boards and synchronized communication modules occasionally freeze, crash, or fail to load real-time comments reliably on certain Android versions.

### **3.3 “Mali mang thai & nuôi dạy con” (Mali Pregnancy & Parenting) App** {#3.3-“mali-mang-thai-&-nuôi-dạy-con”-(mali-pregnancy-&-parenting)-app}

                                   ![][image5]

**Description:**

Mali (Mali Pregnancy & Parenting) is a B2C (Business-to-Consumer) maternal and early childhood tracking mobile application designed to support parents throughout the critical first 1,000 days of a child's life \- from conception until the child reaches two years of age. A primary architectural and content differentiator of Mali compared to Western alternatives is its deeply localized knowledge base, medical insights, and developmental benchmarks, which are specifically tailored to the physical metrics, nutritional habits, and cultural contexts of Asian demographics. The system operates as a standalone mobile journal and informational assistant for families during both the prenatal and postpartum phases. 

**Link:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=me.mali.app](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=me.mali.app) 

**Main features:**

* 1,000-Day Continuous Tracking: Delivers daily and weekly stage-based updates on fetal development and infant growth, extending the user retention lifecycle well beyond childbirth into toddlerhood.  
* Asian-Centric Certified Knowledge Base: Features over 1,000 localized tips and 300+ comprehensive articles reviewed by obstetricians, pediatricians, and child development specialists, calibrated for Asian dietary guidelines and cultural traditions.   
* Standard Pregnancy Utility Toolkit: Incorporates essential interactive tracking tools including a Kick Counter (fetal movement log), Contraction Timer, Due Date Calculator, and a BMI-based maternal weight progression tracker.   
* Postpartum & Newborn Care Journal: Supports daily tracking of infant routines (sleep windows, feeding volumes, diaper change frequencies) and logs physiological developmental milestones.   
* Role-Based Onboarding Personalization: Allows users to select specific roles upon account setup (Mother, Father, Grandmother, or Grandfather) to customize notification streams, tips, and caregiving guidance based on their family role.   
* Interactive Community Forum: Provides a built-in, moderated social space for expectant and postpartum mothers to post anonymous questions, read FAQs, and share real-world parenting experiences. 

**Pros:**

* Long-Term User Retention Strategy: Effectively addresses the common churn issue of pregnancy apps by smoothly transitioning into a highly functional postpartum and toddler development tracker up to age two.   
* Deep Regional Practicality: Nutritional guides, wellness checklists, and lifestyle recommendations are highly relevant and budget-friendly for Southeast Asian markets like Vietnam, fostering strong user relatability.   
* Inclusive Family Engagement: The role-customization feature actively involves fathers and extended family members in the care cycle, mitigating cognitive and emotional burdens on the mother.   
* Credible, Expert-Vetted Content: Educational materials are rigorously screened by a medical advisory board, significantly reducing the exposure to unverified folk remedies or harmful internet misinformation. 

**Cons:**

* Siloed B2C Ecosystem (Lack of Healthcare/Clinic Integration): The platform operates in complete isolation from actual clinical facilities and medical enterprise systems. Health metrics logged by users at home cannot be synchronized via API to private clinic dashboards, preventing attending doctors from executing remote triage or reviewing patient-entered data in real-time.   
* Surface-Level Family Synchronization Architecture: Although external family members can create specialized accounts to read articles, the app lacks a deep data-sharing pipeline. Family members cannot seamlessly co-track or view synchronized, real-time health logs, clinical appointment histories, or daily baby journals across separate devices.   
* Passive Manual Tracking & Lack of IoT Integration: The application depends entirely on the user's voluntary manual data entry. The absence of interoperability with IoT smart wearables (such as health-tracking smartwatches or smart baby monitors) prevents the objective, automated collection of vital signs, increasing clinical risk if an exhausted mother forgets to log data.  
* No Active Emergency Triage or Red Alert Protocols: When critical biometric data or home-logged symptoms fall into high-risk thresholds, the system only displays generic, static textual advice. It completely lacks an automated mechanism to trigger urgent red alerts to designated family members or initiate fast-booking workflows with an associated clinic network.   
* Ad-Supported UX Friction: The free tier relies heavily on invasive video advertisements and monetization banners within core tracking utility views, causing visual clutter and creating user friction during time-sensitive health logging. 

### **3.4 "Bé Của Mẹ" (Mother's Baby) App**  {#3.4-"bé-của-mẹ"-(mother's-baby)-app}

 			![][image6]

**Description** "Bé Của Mẹ" is a comprehensive mobile platform that combines a micro-social network with a medical handbook tailored for mothers. The system covers the entire lifecycle of the target user: from preconception and pregnancy tracking to childbirth and parenting. The application heavily focuses on building a community for sharing experiences and providing a well-categorized knowledge base (Handbook).

**Main Features** Based on the actual application architecture, the system comprises the following core modules:

* **Social & Community Module:**  
  * **Newsfeed:** Displays shared posts and questions from the community, categorized by tabs (Latest, HOT, Useful).  
  * **Age-based Groups:** Allows users to join specialized groups based on their child's birth year (e.g., Baby Rooster 2017, Golden Buffalo 2021\) to facilitate empathetic discussions and relevant knowledge sharing.  
  * **Chat System:** Supports real-time group chat rooms (Moms' Chat, Pregnancy Club).  
* **Knowledge Base Module (CMS):**  
  * Categorizes content into three main phases: *Preconception, Pregnancy, and Parenting*.  
  * Provides specialized articles on: Nutrition, Fetal development by week, Childhood diseases, Wonder Weeks, and Vaccinations.  
* **Personal Tracking Module:**  
  * Manages baby profiles (Estimated Due Date, Gender, Status).  
  * Utility tools for mothers: Menstrual cycle diary and maternal weight tracking.  
  * Journaling feature to save and share milestone moments via photos.  
* **E-commerce/Utility Module:** Manages orders and address books for purchasing maternity and baby products directly within the platform.

**Pros**

* **High User Retention:** Segmenting groups by the child's birth year and featuring real-time chat rooms significantly increases session length and user engagement.  
* **Intelligent Information Architecture:** The UX/UI of the "Handbook" section utilizes a grid layout with intuitive icons, clearly divided by stages. This prevents cognitive overload from massive amounts of text.  
* **Personalization:** The application dynamically adjusts recommended content based on the user's configured status (e.g., current week of pregnancy or the baby's exact age in months).

**Cons**

* **Cluttered UI:** The home screen contains an overwhelming number of functional buttons and tabs, leading to a cramped and visually outdated user interface.  
* **Lack of Automated Trackers:** The system is heavily skewed towards document reading and social networking but lacks dedicated, real-time tracking tools (such as breastfeeding timers, sleep duration trackers, or detailed diaper/formula logs) that modern users frequently require.  
* **Medical Content Moderation Risks:** Due to the open nature of the social network, users might share unverified prescriptions or medical tips, posing information risks. The system lacks a verified badge or authentication system from medical professionals.

## 

## **4\. Business Opportunity** {#4.-business-opportunity}

### **4.1 Market Opportunity and Business Problem** {#4.1-market-opportunity-and-business-problem}

Maternal and early childhood care is a long and continuous journey that extends from pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum recovery, and early childcare. During this journey, mothers, parents, and family caregivers need to remember clinical appointments, vaccination schedules, baby care routines, medical instructions, warning signs, and daily care tasks. However, most of these activities happen outside hospitals or clinics, where families often manage information manually and make daily decisions with limited professional support.

In the current environment, care-related information is highly fragmented. Medical records may be stored as paper documents, ultrasound images in phone galleries, chat messages, personal notes, vaccination books, or separate mobile applications. At the same time, many parents rely on Facebook groups, Zalo groups, public forums, and informal advice from relatives when they have questions about pregnancy, postpartum recovery, breastfeeding, infant symptoms, vaccination, nutrition, or child development. These channels are convenient and familiar, but they are not designed to provide structured health support, verified expert guidance, privacy control, or safe moderation.

This creates a clear business problem: families already have a strong need for digital support, but existing tools do not provide one trusted place to manage the full maternal and early childhood care journey. Without a dedicated platform, users may forget important care tasks, lose health records, misunderstand warning signs, receive unsafe advice, or expose sensitive personal and child-related information in uncontrolled online communities.

CareBridge is proposed to solve this problem by providing a community-based maternal and early childhood health support platform. The system helps users organize personal care information, receive reminders, store health records, track mother and baby care activities, ask questions in a moderated community, access verified content, and connect with verified experts when deeper support is needed.

### **4.2 Market Environment and Existing Solution Gap** {#4.2-market-environment-and-existing-solution-gap}

The market environment for CareBridge is shaped by two major trends. First, Vietnamese families are increasingly familiar with mobile applications, online communities, and digital services for daily life management. Young parents commonly search for parenting, pregnancy, vaccination, nutrition, and childcare information online. Second, public awareness of medical misinformation, privacy risks, and unsafe online advice is increasing, especially when the information relates to mothers, infants, and young children.

Several existing pregnancy and parenting applications already provide useful functions such as pregnancy week tracking, fetal development information, baby journals, checklists, or community forums. These products prove that there is real user demand for digital maternal and childcare support. However, most existing solutions still have important limitations.

Some applications focus mainly on pregnancy tracking and provide limited support after childbirth. Others provide rich educational content but do not connect users with verified experts or structured personal records. Some community-based applications create high engagement, but open community discussions may expose users to unverified medical advice, hidden advertising, or unsafe personal recommendations. In many cases, existing applications operate as standalone tools and do not provide a complete support flow that combines personal records, reminders, baby care journals, moderated Q\&A, expert verification, privacy control, and safe risk orientation.

CareBridge is attractive because it addresses these gaps through an integrated support model. Instead of being only a pregnancy tracker, baby journal, content application, or social group, CareBridge combines care journey management, personal health records, reminders, family coordination, moderated community support, verified expert profiles, verified content, and AI-assisted risk triage within one platform.

### **4.3 Proposed Product Value** {#4.3-proposed-product-value}

CareBridge provides value to users by reducing confusion, forgetfulness, and dependence on unsafe information sources. Mothers and parents can use the platform to follow their care journey, store important records, receive reminders, track baby care routines, and prepare better information before asking experts or visiting healthcare facilities. Family members can receive selected schedules, reminders, and tasks based on permissions granted by the main user, which improves family coordination without exposing all sensitive information.

The moderated community creates another important value. Users can ask questions, share personal experiences, and receive emotional support from people in similar situations. However, unlike open social media groups, CareBridge is designed with report handling, moderation workflows, source labeling, expert badges, and safety boundaries. Community answers are treated as personal experiences, while expert answers are clearly labeled according to professional verification status.

Verified experts also receive value from the platform. Doctors, midwives, nutrition specialists, lactation consultants, psychologists, and child development specialists can build professional profiles, answer selected community questions, contribute trusted content, and receive private consultation requests when appropriate. This creates a practical expert network in which professionals can support the community while also building reputation and future income opportunities.

From a business perspective, CareBridge can begin with free core features to attract users and demonstrate social value. Later, the platform can develop sustainable revenue through optional private consultations, expert marketplace commission, premium utilities, social impact campaigns, CSR programs and cooperation with healthcare-related organizations. The platform should not depend on selling personal health data. Instead, its business potential comes from trust, user retention, expert participation, and value-added services.

### **4.4 Initial Adoption Strategy and Scalability** {#4.4-initial-adoption-strategy-and-scalability}

CareBridge should initially focus on users in major urban areas such as Ha Noi, Hai Phong, and Ho Chi Minh City. These cities have a higher concentration of young families, maternity services, pediatric clinics, private healthcare providers, and users who are familiar with digital services. This geographic focus is not the project scope itself. It is an initial adoption strategy used to validate user demand, collect feedback, test community moderation, onboard verified experts, and improve the product before wider expansion.

The first adoption group should include pre-pregnancy women, pregnant women, postpartum mothers, parents of infants and young children, spouses, family caregivers, and verified experts. The system should be introduced as a maternal and early childhood care support platform, not as a hospital system, official electronic medical record system, emergency service, diagnosis tool, or prescription platform.

As the product becomes stable, CareBridge can gradually expand beyond the initial cities to other provinces and broader healthcare-related professional networks. This expansion should depend on the platform’s ability to maintain safe community governance, verify experts, protect personal data, scale storage and notifications, manage moderation workload, and provide reliable support to a growing number of users.

In the long term, CareBridge can fit with broader digital health and social impact trends by helping families manage care information more safely, helping experts reach users in a controlled environment, and helping healthcare organizations support maternal and early childhood health education. The product is therefore attractive because it solves a real daily-life problem, fits existing digital behavior, improves safety compared with uncontrolled online communities, and creates a foundation for sustainable growth.

## **5\. Software Product Vision** {#5.-software-product-vision}

### **5.1 Vision Statement** {#5.1-vision-statement}
